segments.text: Header of the kernel `read_1pl`. The name means one load per 64 B line. The whole-chip test times it in part L and in control I, as the last kernel of the sequence [Ref9].
segments.heading: Kernel `read_1pl`: one 16 B load per 64 B, function `k_read_1pl`

segments.text:
Start address `55d0` (hexadecimal) and name of the function. **The loop is lines 757 to 763.**
- Address range: `55d4` to `55ec`. That is 7 instructions, 28 bytes of code. Loop start modulo 64: 20.
- Bytes read per loop pass: 64 B. The pointer moves 256 B per pass.
- Load instructions per loop pass: 4 (`ldr`, 16 B each).
- Other instructions per loop pass: 3 (`add`, `cmp`, `b.cc`).
- The loaded values are not used.
- Source: the asm text of the function `k_read_1pl` in bwx12.c [Ref6].

This instruction runs once per call, before the loop. It computes the end address `x1 = x0 + 8 * n`. The compiler wrote it.
- The function stores no register on the stack.
- Reason: the loop names `q0` to `q3` only. The source comment says that gcc saves nothing for them [Ref6].

The loop starts at line 757. Each `ldr` loads 16 B into one vector register. The offsets are 0, 64, 128 and 192 B from `x0`.
- So one pass reads bytes 0 to 15 of each of four 64 B lines, and no other byte [Ref6].
- bwx12 counts the whole length of the range that a call covers. So the rate of this kernel counts 256 B per loop pass, and the loop loads 64 B of them [Ref8].
Moves the pointer forward by 256 B (`0x100` = 256).
`cmp x0, x1` compares the pointer with the end address. `b.cc 55d4` jumps back to line 757 while the pointer is lower (unsigned compare).
`ret` returns to the caller. The function returns no value.
